text: Azure RBAC's mechanics — principal, role definition, scope — came up in an earlier course. This lesson is about something that applies on any platform running role-based access control: how do you actually decide what the roles themselves should be, in a real organization, instead of just in theory?

The most common approach is also the wrong one: clone an existing user's access for a new hire doing "basically the same job." That copies whatever accumulated on the original account, including anything over-granted or left over from a role they no longer hold. The right question is simpler — what does this job function actually require? Build the role from that answer.

Role mining, or role discovery, means analyzing real permission usage and job responsibilities to find the role groupings an organization already has informally. Pull a report of what a department actually uses, group the users whose real patterns cluster together, and propose that cluster as a formal role — discovered from evidence, not invented from an org chart.

A role built this way looks like Billing-Support-Tier1: read access to tickets, read-only customer lookups, and refunds capped at fifty dollars, assigned to twelve users. Nothing in it is a copy of any one person's account — every line maps back to something the job function genuinely needs.

Role explosion is the opposite failure: every small variation in access gets its own dedicated role instead of reusing a shared base. A twelve-person support team ends up with twelve nearly-identical roles, each differing by a permission or two, and now nobody can audit any of them. The fix is discipline — keep roles few and well-defined, and handle a genuine one-off need as a scoped, time-limited exception, not a permanent new role.

RBAC assigns the same fixed permissions to everyone holding a role, which breaks down the moment access needs to depend on something that changes — the time of day, the device being used, how sensitive the resource is. That's where attribute-based access control picks up next.
